method: OPEN AND QUOTED from Italian medical oncology expert panel (Adamo V, et al.), Supportive Care in Cancer 2022;30:9877 'Supportive therapies in the prevention of chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenia and appropriate use of granulocyte colony-stimulating factors: a Delphi consensus statement' (published 5 November 2022). Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC9715510).

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Febrile neutropenia is an oncological emergency:** fever above 38.3 °C (or above 38.0 °C twice over 2 h), or signs of sepsis, with a neutrophil count below 0.5, or below 1.0 and expected to fall. A lower reading of 38 °C lasting 1 h can also count.
claims.source_text: Febrile neutropenia (FN) is the most significant complication of neutropenia constituting an oncological emergency and is defined as the appearance of fever (oral temperature > 38.3 °C or two consecutive readings of > 38.0 °C for 2 h) or clinical signs of sepsis in a patient with a neutrophil count of < 0.5 × 109/L (< 500/mm3) or < 1.0 × 109/L (< 1000/mm3) prenadir … a lower oral temperature (38 °C) sustained for 1 h can be considered FN
claims.locator: Italian medical oncology expert panel (Adamo V, et al.), Supportive Care in Cancer 2022;30:9877, 'Supportive therapies in the prevention of chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenia and appropriate use of granulocyte colony-stimulating factors: a Delphi consensus statement', published 5 November 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9715510/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **FN incidence ranges from 2 to 50%,** set by patient factors (age, comorbidity, organ dysfunction, performance status, marrow reserve), cancer type, regimen and genetics. Serious complications reach 25–30% and mortality 9–12% in high-risk groups.
claims.source_text: The incidence of FN varies between 2 and 50% depending on patient-related risk factors (e.g. age, neutropenia, major comorbidities, liver or kidney dysfunction, poor performance status, other concurrent immunosuppression or other reasons for compromised bone marrow function), cancer type, chemotherapy regimen (e.g. planned full dose intensity > 85%), and genetic susceptibility, which also influences its clinical outcome [, ]. While most patients experience mild episodes, the rate of serious complications (25-30%) and mortality (9-12%) remains elevated in high-risk groups
claims.locator: Italian medical oncology expert panel (Adamo V, et al.), Supportive Care in Cancer 2022;30:9877, 'Supportive therapies in the prevention of chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenia and appropriate use of granulocyte colony-stimulating factors: a Delphi consensus statement', published 5 November 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9715510/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Neutropenia severity follows chemotherapy intensity,** and the nadir usually falls between days 7 and 14 after the first dose.
claims.source_text: there is adequate evidence that the severity of neutropenia is dependent on the intensity of the chemotherapy regimen (defined by the type, dose, and number of myelosuppressive cytotoxic agents in a chemotherapy regimen) … which in most patient is a nadir between days 7-14 after the first dose
claims.locator: Italian medical oncology expert panel (Adamo V, et al.), Supportive Care in Cancer 2022;30:9877, 'Supportive therapies in the prevention of chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenia and appropriate use of granulocyte colony-stimulating factors: a Delphi consensus statement', published 5 November 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9715510/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Assess FN risk at the start of every chemotherapy cycle,** and fit the regimen to the patient's characteristics and treatment goals.
claims.source_text: Current guidelines suggest assessing FN risk at the start of each chemotherapy cycle in order to prevent or better manage the condition if it arises. … the chemotherapy regimen should be based on the patient's clinical characteristics and treatment goals after the evaluation of the risk of FN to ensure appropriate treatment
claims.locator: Italian medical oncology expert panel (Adamo V, et al.), Supportive Care in Cancer 2022;30:9877, 'Supportive therapies in the prevention of chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenia and appropriate use of granulocyte colony-stimulating factors: a Delphi consensus statement', published 5 November 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9715510/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Adding immunotherapy to chemotherapy does not raise FN risk,** so use the same criteria as for chemotherapy alone.
claims.source_text: There was consensus that the incidence of FN was not increased when chemotherapy was combined with immunotherapy (compared with chemotherapy alone); therefore, physicians should use the same criteria to decide on chemo-immunotherapy as they would for chemotherapy (item 7)
claims.locator: Italian medical oncology expert panel (Adamo V, et al.), Supportive Care in Cancer 2022;30:9877, 'Supportive therapies in the prevention of chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenia and appropriate use of granulocyte colony-stimulating factors: a Delphi consensus statement', published 5 November 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9715510/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Check nutritional status before chemotherapy:** poor nutrition raises marrow toxicity. Neutropenic diets do not reduce FN.
claims.source_text: a patient's nutritional status should be assessed prior to initiating a chemotherapy program, considering that poor nutritional status increases the risk of bone marrow toxicity (item 8) … According to a meta-analysis of RCTs, neutropenic diets do not reduce the risk of FN
claims.locator: Italian medical oncology expert panel (Adamo V, et al.), Supportive Care in Cancer 2022;30:9877, 'Supportive therapies in the prevention of chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenia and appropriate use of granulocyte colony-stimulating factors: a Delphi consensus statement', published 5 November 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9715510/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Primary prophylaxis when FN risk is 20% or more;** consider it at 10–20% depending on the patient.
claims.source_text: primary prophylaxis with G-CSF should be considered in patients with a ≥ 20% risk of chemotherapy-induced FN to reduce FN-related complications and to avoid chemotherapy dose reduction (items 32 and 33), as well as in patients with 10-20% risk of developing FN, depending on the patient's clinical characteristics (item 34)
claims.locator: Italian medical oncology expert panel (Adamo V, et al.), Supportive Care in Cancer 2022;30:9877, 'Supportive therapies in the prevention of chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenia and appropriate use of granulocyte colony-stimulating factors: a Delphi consensus statement', published 5 November 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9715510/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Factors that push intermediate (10–20%) risk towards prophylaxis:** age over 65, advanced disease, poor performance status, liver or kidney dysfunction, recent extensive surgery, persistent neutropenia, prior FN, poor nutrition, bone marrow involvement, multimorbidity or frailty, or when an episode would be especially dangerous.
claims.source_text: when there is an intermediate risk (10-20%), but the risk of FN is increased (patient aged > 65 years, advanced disease, poor performance status, liver or kidney dysfunction, recent extensive surgery, persistent neutropenia, prior episodes of FN, poor nutritional status, widespread bone marrow involvement, multimorbidity, or frailty), or when the consequences of the neutropenic episode are foreseen to be more severe
claims.locator: Italian medical oncology expert panel (Adamo V, et al.), Supportive Care in Cancer 2022;30:9877, 'Supportive therapies in the prevention of chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenia and appropriate use of granulocyte colony-stimulating factors: a Delphi consensus statement', published 5 November 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9715510/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Not recommended as primary prophylaxis below 10% risk.**
claims.source_text: These guidelines do not recommend G-CSF as primary prophylaxis in patients with < 10% risk of FN
claims.locator: Italian medical oncology expert panel (Adamo V, et al.), Supportive Care in Cancer 2022;30:9877, 'Supportive therapies in the prevention of chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenia and appropriate use of granulocyte colony-stimulating factors: a Delphi consensus statement', published 5 November 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9715510/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Long-acting G-CSF suits primary and secondary prophylaxis** when the regimen can drop neutrophils to 500 cells/μL or below and keeping dose intensity matters.
claims.source_text: The panel also agreed that it is appropriate to use long-acting G-CSF in primary and secondary prophylaxis during chemotherapy regimens with the potential to induce neutropenia of ≤ 500 cells/μL when the treatment goal correlates with maintenance of dose intensity (item 36)
claims.locator: Italian medical oncology expert panel (Adamo V, et al.), Supportive Care in Cancer 2022;30:9877, 'Supportive therapies in the prevention of chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenia and appropriate use of granulocyte colony-stimulating factors: a Delphi consensus statement', published 5 November 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9715510/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Using G-CSF instead of cutting chemotherapy dose is an accepted alternative;** primary prophylaxis reduced all-cause mortality in a meta-analysis, especially with dose-dense chemotherapy.
claims.source_text: An alternative approach then is to use G-CSF rather than changing the dose intensity of the chemotherapeutic agents … A systemic review and meta-analysis of RCTs comparing chemotherapy with or without primary prophylaxis with G-CSF showed a significant reduction in all-cause mortality with G-CSF therapy, particularly in patients receiving dose-dense chemotherapy
claims.locator: Italian medical oncology expert panel (Adamo V, et al.), Supportive Care in Cancer 2022;30:9877, 'Supportive therapies in the prevention of chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenia and appropriate use of granulocyte colony-stimulating factors: a Delphi consensus statement', published 5 November 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9715510/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Biosimilar G-CSFs are appropriate for routine use;** their activity and toxicity match the originators.
claims.source_text: The panel reached a consensus on the use of biosimilar G-CSFs in routine clinical practice (Table 2) as they agreed that the activity and toxicity profiles of biosimilar G-CSFs were comparable with those of the original G-CSFs (item 9)
claims.locator: Italian medical oncology expert panel (Adamo V, et al.), Supportive Care in Cancer 2022;30:9877, 'Supportive therapies in the prevention of chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenia and appropriate use of granulocyte colony-stimulating factors: a Delphi consensus statement', published 5 November 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9715510/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Filgrastim 5 μg/kg daily until post-nadir recovery (up to 14 days), or pegfilgrastim 6 mg once per cycle.** Long-acting forms help patients with poor adherence and reduce severe neutropenia and FN.
claims.source_text: They also agreed that long-acting formulations of G-CSFs are effective in patients with poor adherence (item 13) and offer an advantage in reducing severe neutropenia and FN (item 15) … Contrary to the daily administration of filgrastim (5 μg/kg; short-acting G-CSF) until post-nadir ANC recovery to near normal levels (which may take up to 14 days), pegfilgrastim is administered as a single subcutaneous injection (6 mg) once after each chemotherapy cycle
claims.locator: Italian medical oncology expert panel (Adamo V, et al.), Supportive Care in Cancer 2022;30:9877, 'Supportive therapies in the prevention of chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenia and appropriate use of granulocyte colony-stimulating factors: a Delphi consensus statement', published 5 November 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9715510/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Give long-acting G-CSF 24 to 72 h after chemotherapy,** not on the same day: same-day pegfilgrastim had higher FN rates in more than 45,000 adults.
claims.source_text: the consensus was achieved on the administration of a long-acting G-CSF 24 to 72 h after chemotherapy administration (item 24) … In a large-scale evaluation of > 45,000 adults who received intermediate/high-risk regimens for solid tumours or non-Hodgkin lymphoma, FN incidence was significantly higher among those who received pegfilgrastim prophylaxis on the same day as chemotherapy completion versus 24-72 h after chemotherapy completion
claims.locator: Italian medical oncology expert panel (Adamo V, et al.), Supportive Care in Cancer 2022;30:9877, 'Supportive therapies in the prevention of chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenia and appropriate use of granulocyte colony-stimulating factors: a Delphi consensus statement', published 5 November 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9715510/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Too-short courses of short-acting G-CSF raise FN risk** and worsen neutropenic outcomes.
claims.source_text: A shorter duration of prophylaxis with short-acting G-CSF was found to increase the risk of FN and lead to worse neutropenia-related clinical outcomes
claims.locator: Italian medical oncology expert panel (Adamo V, et al.), Supportive Care in Cancer 2022;30:9877, 'Supportive therapies in the prevention of chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenia and appropriate use of granulocyte colony-stimulating factors: a Delphi consensus statement', published 5 November 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9715510/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Bone pain affects 25 to 38%.** Treat first with paracetamol or an NSAID (e.g. naproxen); antihistamines (e.g. loratadine), opioids or G-CSF dose reduction are second line.
claims.source_text: Bone pain is the commonly reported AE associated with G-CSF use, ranging from 25 to 38%. First-line treatment for bone pain involves acetaminophen and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents (e.g. naproxen), while antihistamines (e.g. loratadine), opioids, and dose reduction of G-CSFs are considered second-line therapy
claims.locator: Italian medical oncology expert panel (Adamo V, et al.), Supportive Care in Cancer 2022;30:9877, 'Supportive therapies in the prevention of chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenia and appropriate use of granulocyte colony-stimulating factors: a Delphi consensus statement', published 5 November 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9715510/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Rare large-vessel vasculitis (about 0.5%)** can occur, sometimes with aortic dissection or aneurysm.
claims.source_text: there are also reports of G-CSF-associated vasculitis that may be accompanied by severe complications like aortic dissection and aneurysm formation … A G-CSF-associated vasculitis is a rare event, with an incidence of 0.5%
claims.locator: Italian medical oncology expert panel (Adamo V, et al.), Supportive Care in Cancer 2022;30:9877, 'Supportive therapies in the prevention of chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenia and appropriate use of granulocyte colony-stimulating factors: a Delphi consensus statement', published 5 November 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9715510/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **FN carries real mortality:** 6.8 to 20% among patients admitted with FN complications, higher with comorbidity, sepsis or shock.
claims.source_text: with estimates of 6.8 to 20% mortality among patients who are hospitalised for FN-related complications and with higher rates observed in patients who have major comorbidities and documented sepsis or shock
claims.locator: Italian medical oncology expert panel (Adamo V, et al.), Supportive Care in Cancer 2022;30:9877, 'Supportive therapies in the prevention of chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenia and appropriate use of granulocyte colony-stimulating factors: a Delphi consensus statement', published 5 November 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9715510/, retrieved 2026-09-23
